newsitem.title: TURKEY: TURKEY MAY GO FOR NEW EURO ISSUE; BANKS IN MARKET.
newsitem.headline: TURKEY MAY GO FOR NEW EURO ISSUE; BANKS IN MARKET.

text.p: After two successful deals in mark and Italian lira earlier this year, bankers say Turkey may go for another Eurobond issue next month or in early April.
"The Turkish treasury should continue to borrow in the international markets to reach its 1997 borrowing target. It may go for another Euro deal," said a senior banker who declined to be named.
"The next issue might be in dollars," he said.
Turkish government officials said the treasury had received new bond issue offers from international banks. They declined to give any further details.

Turkey issued 300 billion lira of five-year Eurobonds earlier this month -- its first issue in the Italian currency. It also raised 500 million marks in January through a seven-year issue, despite concerns that Moody's could yet downgrade the country's Ba3 credit rating.
Standard and Poor's, JCR and IBCA cut Turkey's rating in late 1996 and early 1997.
Turkish officials say the markets have already discounted potential Moody's credit rating of one notch down and reflected it in the pricing.

"After the S&P downgrading, creditors readjusted their pricings in line with the cut. Moody's will probably bring its rating down to the S&P level if it decides to cut our rating, and this will not make so much change for us," a government official told Reuters.
"But if Moody's lowers the rating below the S&P level, which seems very unlikely to me, then it might be a problem," the official said.
Turkey presently has a single B rating from S&P.
Bankers say any bigger-than-expected downgrading by Moody's may delay Turkey's borrowing plan for the new issue.
A senior analyst with Moody's said on Wednesday that Turkey's foreign currency rating is set for either a downgrade or confirmation in the near future.
He said concerns about Turkey's fiscal policy in general prompted Moody's to place the country's foreign currency rating under review on January 9.
Turkey is planning to borrow at least $2 billion this year. The country's foreign debt stock stood at $78.04 billion at end-September.
Apart from the government's plan for new borrowings, some Turkish banks and companies have also stepped into the foreign loan markets.

Banking sources say private Finansbank and Garanti Bankasi are in the market to launch syndicated loans. Garanti is expected to launch a $150 million loan to help financing of a motorway project undertaken by Garanti's majority owner Dogus group. Garanti officials are not immediately available for confirmation.

Finansbank launched a $30 million one-year syndicated loan on Thursday, bank officials said. The deal, arranged by Standard and Chartered, Sakura and West LB, will have an interest of LIBOR plus 90 basis points.

Turkish cellular phone company Turkcell is also planning a $570 million loan to be used in its payment for licences of Global System of Mobile (GSM) telephone network and some other investments, officials from Cukurova group, which owns Turkcell, said.
Cukurova group is also in the market for a $125 million syndicated loan, group co-ordinator Mehmet Gur had told Reuters earlier this week. Gur said SBC Warburg was leading the syndication.
